newsitem.title: GERMANY: Plans set for NATO summit, charter with Russia.
newsitem.headline: Plans set for NATO summit, charter with Russia.

text.p: NATO leaders will hold a summit next year to formally decide new members and approve a charter defining the alliance relationship with Russia, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and other officials said on Friday.

In a speech outlining the U.S. vision of a "new Atlantic Community", Christopher also said negotiations should begin with other potential NATO candidates once first-round new members are chosen and he proposed ways to strengthen NATO's "partnership for peace" programme.

He said the new "community" should extend to central Europe and newly independent states, including Russia, "transcending the artificial boundaries of Cold War Europe (and giving) North America a deeper partnership with a broader, more integrated Europe."
Germany is "heart of an increasingly united continent" and "symbol and a catalyst" for European integration, he said.
Christopher spoke on the 50th anniversary of a speech in this city by then secretary of state James Byrnes after World War Two that was a turning point in U.S.-German relations.

Byrnes made clear then that the United States, which isolated itself after World War I, would remain engaged in Europe and he put the Americans firmly on the side of restoring German political and economy unity.
Such principles "shape our approach to Europe this very day," Christopher said.

As part of a long-scheduled plan, NATO foreign ministers are to meet in December in Brussels on alliance expansion eastward, internal adaption of NATO to meet new post-Cold War challenges and its relationship to Russia.
U.S. officials said that will not be a decision-making meeting but only "set the stage" for a NATO summit in 1997.

NATO leaders embraced a comprehensive strategy for European security in January 1994 and now President Clinton believes another summit is needed to "complete the implementation of this strategy," Christopher said.

Hence, "I expect our leaders will meet in the spring or early summer of 1997 (and) we should invite several partners to begin accession negotiations," he said. A summit date and place has not been set but the venue is expected to be Europe.
Countries viewed as topping the list for first-round NATO membership are Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Officials had been saying for months a NATO summit would be held early in 1997. The possible delay until summer apparently is to give more time to negotiations with Russia.

Giving hope to countries not selected in the first round, Christopher said the door to NATO membership will stay open "for all those who demonstrate that they are willing and able to shoulder the responsibilities of membership."
"NATO should enter a new phase of its intensified dialogues with all those who continue to seek membership after the first candidates are invited to join," he said.

Although Russia has long fought NATO plans to take in new members from former Warsaw Pact states, U.S. officials said Moscow is now intensely engaged in discussions with the alliance on a long-term Russia-NATO relationship.

Christopher more explicitly than before asserted that "NATO's cooperation with Russia should be expressed in a formal charter" because a mechanism is needed to respond immediately to crises like Bosnia.

Officials told reporters they expect the summit to approve such a charter and that Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov has done a good job defining for the allies the Russian national interests that must be considered in their new relationship.

U.S. officials said the summit would mark the culmination of NATO's efforts to transform itself to meet new post-Cold War challenges, including full integration of France and Spain into the alliance's military wing.

Christopher said NATO's partnership for peace programme of cooperation with Russia and other former communist states should involve non-NATO members in planning as well as execution of NATO missions in a new Atlantic Partnership Council. Its missions should also be expanded, he said.

He stressed the need for greater economic integration and swift enlargement of the European Union. Cold War divisions of Europe are fading but are still visible in the "economic gulf between east and west," he said.

He made brief reference to U.S.-European differences over U.S. sanctions imposed on those who do business with Iran and Libya. "Working together against state sponsors of terrorism is an imperative, not an option," he said.
